articles.title: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
articles.summary: It comes after the armed group hit Riyadh's international airport and another facility, killing 13 people, in a significant escalation.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed a "serious" response to the deadly attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement.

"The events of recent weeks are serious. Our response must be equally serious," Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh.

On Sunday, a Pakistani man was killed in an attack on a terminal at the capital's King Khalid International Airport, Saudi authorities said. It came a day after a Houthi missile hit another terminal, killing 13 people and forcing its closure.

The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for "brutal Saudi aggression" against areas they control in western Yemen.

The Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six other people were injured in a Saudi air strike on a home in the capital, Sanaa, on Sunday.

A Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces battling the Houthis on Yemen's Red Sea coast and other areas.

The WPC Energy Congress opened on Sunday at a convention centre about 10km (6 miles) from Riyadh's airport, which has been attacked four times over the past week.

Last Thursday, three Saudis, including a pilot for the national airline Saudia, were killed in two strikes on an airport facility and an aircraft on the ground.

Another four Saudis, as well as two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian, one Sudanese and one Indian, were killed in Saturday's missile strike on Terminal 3.

On Sunday, a Pakistani resident was killed when a projectile hit Terminal 4, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).

King Fahd International Airport in the north-eastern city of Dammam was also attacked on Sunday evening, it said, but no casualties were reported.

Later, the Saudi-led coalition said its forces had intercepted a drone in Eastern Province and a missile launched by the Houthis towards the south-western city of Khamis Mushait.

In his inaugural address to the WPC Energy Congress on Monday, Prince Abdul Aziz thanked industry executives and policymakers for attending despite the attacks.

"You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart," he said.

But he also acknowledged that "energy security cannot be taken for granted" and that recent developments had "tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience".

Prince Abdul Aziz promised that his country would overcome those challenges.

"We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people," he said. "We shall prove it to the world that whatever we are going through we will overcome it."

There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.

On Sunday evening, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a video statement that its forces had launched missiles and drones at Riyadh and Dammam's airports, as well as two oil and gas facilities in Eastern Province, in response to 124 Saudi air strikes in Yemen over the previous 24 hours.

Sarea also reiterated a warning to airlines and passengers against using Saudi airports and airspace, except for journeys to and from the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina.

The Houthis' forces, he vowed, would "continue their escalating operations deep inside Saudi, imposing the equation of 'a blockade for a blockade' and 'an escalation for an escalation' and targeting Saudi enemy reinforcements until the aggression ceases and the siege on our dear people is lifted".

Saturday's attack on Riyadh airport drew widespread international condemnation.

UN Secretary General António Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" and warned that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure were a violation of international law.

President Donald Trump said he would "make a decision" about the US joining Saudi Arabia's strikes on the Houthis. The US military is reportedly already providing intelligence and targeting support to the Saudi-led coalition.

Iran, which has repeatedly denied allegations that it provides weapons and training to the Houthis, said it was "deeply concerned" by the escalation and called for "dialogue and engagement" to resolve the situation.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing.

Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea.

They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.

Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

articles.body: A six-year-old girl living beneath one of Europe's most active volcanoes recently became the only pupil at a school that the Italian media is calling the smallest in Europe and where the bell hadn't rung for the past 20 years. On September 10, 2026, Aysha went off to her first day of school in Ginostra, a tiny hamlet on the side of the Stromboli volcano, with a pink backpack and a cone of sweets in her hands. According to Italian news agency ANSA, she was visibly moved as her parents walked her in to meet her teacher, Laura Mongi, who had come down from the outskirts of Milan.An island inside an islandThe fishing hamlet of Ginostra is part of the town of Lipari, on the Italian island of Stromboli is so isolated that residents have christened it 'the island within an island.' With no roads connecting it to the rest of the island and access only by boat, the community is often left cut off from the rest of the world.A donkey takes care of the logistics, and water comes in by a tanker. The village once had its own primary school, but it closed decades ago when the population dwindled to around 40 residents. "The town of Lipari is spread across six different islands, Lipari, Vulcano, Stromboli, Panarea, Filicudi and Alicudi, plus the hamlet of Ginostra, which is an island in the island: even though it's on Stromboli, it's connected only by sea," Abbate, who's the town's delegate, told the magazine Vita in February.A letter for homeAbbate told Sicilian daily La Sicilia in January that the family would have been forced to split up. "My husband, who has a small construction company, would have had to stay here; me and the child would have had to move,” she said. “To get to Lipari we had to get up at dawn, take the hydrofoil and come back in the afternoon. But in winter it often happens that we stay stuck because of storm surges, so school attendance wasn’t guaranteed.”Abbate and Bazine, who were born and raised in Mazara del Vallo in western Sicily and has lived in Ginostra for 16 years, according to Vita. They wrote to the mayor, to the head of the Lipari comprehensive school, Patrizia Muscolino, and to the provincial school office in Messina. “Everything started when we wrote a letter explaining all the hardships we have on the island and how impossible it was to get to the other schools,” Abbate told Open. “I’d already talked about it several times in the years before; I was very determined about this choice.”Lipari’s town government filed the formal request on January 8, and the regional school office for Sicily said yes on January 19, according to the education site Orizzonte Scuola. Italian law normally asks for at least 15 pupils to open a primary class, though exceptions are allowed in places at risk of depopulation.Now local authorities have agreed to reopen it after Aysha's parents warned they would have been forced to leave the island. The six-year-old would have to travel to a school in Lipari, the largest island on the Aeolian archipelago. Her parents, Monica Abbate and Raffa Bazine, say they have no intention to leave and insist their daughter is happy as the sole student.She isn’t planning on going anywhere, though. “It’s a bare-bones life. You don’t have the comforts of the city: we have just one grocery store that’s open all year,” she told Open. “But here you figure out what the real priorities are, and everything gets freer, less driven by consumerism. My daughter is growing up close to nature; here you always get around on foot. I’d never change my life.”"We love this little paradise, the nature, the sea, even the volcano that looms over our homes. We don't want to have to leave," Bazine told Italian news outlet Ansa. "She hangs out with peers who stay here for months at a time, and she's learned a few words of German from the neighbours' children who go on vacation in Ginostra. She's a happy child," the parents said.“Emergencies? We’ve had plenty of them with the floods of recent years,” Abbate told Vita. “And then we’re under an active volcano, so for us it’s always staying on alert. Do I think it’s dangerous? I think there are many more dangers in the city.” On Etna, Sicily’s other famous volcano, skiers kept carving turns in December 2025 even as ash and smoke rose behind the ridge line.A school for a studentThe new school will feature a single classroom in a building owned by the local parish of the Catholic Church. "The opening of the school is 'a sign of solidarity for this isolated community'," said Riccardo Gullo, the village's mayor. "Schooling should be 'a fundamental right', even for people living in remote areas," he added.Father Nino Pirrotta, the parish priest, said, "Schools are not just a place of learning; they are a focus for the community."The teacher will follow a customised ministerial program, marking a significant precedent for the protection of the right to education in geographically disadvantaged areas and in combating the depopulation of small Italian towns.Whether the school stays open beyond Aysha’s first year depends on how many pupils enrol in the years ahead, since a full primary cycle requires steady attendance numbers. Families on nearby islands such as Filicudi still face serious schooling gaps, showing that Ginostra’s success has not yet spread across the region. Officials have been clear that the current setup meets one family’s specific need, and broader policy changes for isolated communities remain an open question.You use AI every day. articles.title: Russell Brand arrives at a London court for his trial on rape and sexual assault charges
articles.summary: LONDON — Comedian Russell Brand arrived at a London court Monday for the opening of his trial on charges of rape and sexual assault.
articles.body: LONDON — Comedian Russell Brand arrived at a London court Monday for the opening of his trial on charges of rape and sexual assault. Brand was flanked by security guards and accompanied by his wife, Laura Gallacher, as he arrived at Southwark Crown Court for the first day of a trial that is expected to last 10 to 12 weeks. Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault. The offenses relate to six women and are alleged to have taken place between 1999 and 2009. He has remained free on bail ahead of his trial. Prosecutors have said at previous hearings that Brand is accused of raping a woman in a hotel room at a Labour Party conference, grabbing a TV worker’s breasts and forcing her into a sex act in a toilet, and kissing and groping a radio station worker. Known for risque stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand was a major star of the early 2000s, with TV hosting jobs, his own BBC radio show and roles in films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek.” In recent years he has dropped out of mainstream media, moved to Florida and built a large following online with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.

articles.title: Hurricane Simon pounds resorts and vulnerable towns along Mexico’s Pacific coast
articles.summary: PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico — Hurricane Simon pounded Mexico’s Pacific coast as a Category 3 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean.
articles.body: PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico — Hurricane Simon pounded Mexico’s Pacific coast as a Category 3 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean. The hurricane’s center swirled parallel to the coast, closing in on the Puerto Vallarta area, where its most damaging winds and rain were expected to hit around midnight and continue through Monday morning. Its maximum sustained winds weakened late Sunday to 115 mph (185 kph), according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami, but it was still expected to remain a dangerous hurricane. That’s not good news for people in and around Puerto Vallarta, a popular tourist destination in the state of Jalisco. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm. By late Sunday, Simon’s eye was moving northwest about 45 miles (75 kilometers) south of Cabo Corrientes at about 5 mph (7 kph). A senior hurricane center specialist, Philippe Papin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system. Cabo Corrientes is at the southern tip of Bahia de Banderas, the wide bay where Puerto Vallarta looks out to the Pacific. Forecasters powerful winds will sweep from Mexico’s western coast to the Sierra Madre Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 15 miles (30 kilometers), and tropical-storm-force winds reach up to 60 miles (95 kilometers) from Simon’s center, meaning the entire area between Mexico’s western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected. “We’re expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west-central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect,” Papin said. “They’re also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that’s likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells.” The hurricane center said Simon was expected to dump an additional 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 centimeters) of rain, with some areas getting up to 8 inches (20 centimeters), in the states of Colima, Jalisco, Nayarit and Sinaloa through early Thursday. Isolated totals of 30 inches (76 centimeters) were possible parts in Michoacan, Colima, and Jalisco states, producing life-threatening flooding and mudslides, the center said. Mexico’s president urges residents to stay sheltered As the storm approached Puerto Vallarta, National Guard vehicles patrolled the streets while police used a megaphone to call out the few people who were jogging, walking their dogs or biking by the waterfront. Officers reminded people that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter. Not everyone followed the orders. Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas while asking the tourism sector to make sure workers and visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum took to the social platform X on Sunday to urge people in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to stay sheltered until the government issues a notification that the danger has passed. She also asked people to follow recommendations from civil protection officials and to avoid traveling on public roads. “Precautionary evacuation efforts to safe zones are ongoing; the priority is our safety,” she wrote. Hotel worker says residents learned from major hurricane in 2002 Hotel worker Víctor Martínez went shopping for nonperishable food Sunday afternoon. He said he could not go to work because public transportation service was suspended and most of the hotel had been evacuated. Martínez found people’s concerns about the hurricane comforting. “It happened to us before. It hit us years ago,” Martínez said, referring to a Category 5 hurricane that hit the area in 2002. “People didn’t expect it. We were very skeptical that it would ever hit us. Now, though, we’re different. Precautions are being taken. It happened to us once, and we won’t let it happen again.” Despite the risks posed by Simon, tourists were still arriving in Puerto Vallarta. Visitors Ricardo Ramírez and Brenda Villarreal, who have never lived through a hurricane, went looking for food by the city’s boardwalk and came across police urging people to take shelter. Ramírez said they were completely unprepared for the situation. “The boardwalk is closed. Be responsible. Understand!” police told passersby using a megaphone. Ramírez said he and Villarreal had planned their four-day vacation since last year and traveled from Guadalajara, Jalisco’s capital. “We don’t know the extent of the danger yet,” Villarreal said. “We’re just starting to see what’s going on.”

articles.title: Giants Brigades lead southern Yemen fightback against the Houthis
articles.summary: Yemen’s Southern Giants Brigades have emerged as one of the leading forces against the Houthis.
articles.body:
On October 5, groups linked to the former Southern Transitional Council (STC), including the powerful Southern Giants Brigades , and troops of the internationally recognised government of Yemen, launched a major offensive against the Houthis near the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb strait.

It was part of a nationwide military campaign aimed at driving the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God, out of territories under their control, including the vital coastline region seized by the Iran-linked group in September.

By Monday afternoon, the pro-government force, led by the Giants Brigade, said they had managed to cut off the main road linking the Red Sea port city of Mocha with the Bab al-Mandeb, a vital waterway for energy supplies.

This effectively gave the anti-Houthi forces one of their first major military gains in years and followed an announcement by Rashid al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), of a major offensive against the Iran-backed group. It also highlighted the effectiveness of anti-Houthi forces – which include units with contrasting political goals – when working together.

This has seen STC-affiliated groups, some of whom seek independence for the south, ally with pro-government national forces against the Houthis.

The collaboration between these two factions follows a high-profile conflict in southern Yemen in January , when Saudi-aligned Yemeni government forces defeated the United Arab Emirates-backed STC, resulting in the relative centralisation of anti-Houthi forces.

Among the leading formations in the recent government offensive led by this alliance are the Giants Brigades, which have their roots in the southern separatist movement.

The force is commanded by Abd al-Rahman Abu Zaraa al-Muharrami , a Salafi who studied at the ultraconservative Dammaj religious school in the northern governorate of Saada.

Formed largely by Salafi fighters during the battle against the Houthis in the southern city of Aden in the first half of 2015, the Giants Brigades have become one of Yemen’s most formidable military forces during the war.

The brigades, believed to have been armed, trained and funded by the UAE, rose to prominence in 2017, leading an offensive that captured large swaths of Yemen’s western coast from the Houthis. The advance was eventually halted on the outskirts of the Red Sea port city of Hodeidah following the United Nations-brokered Stockholm Agreement in late 2018.

In January 2022, the Giants Brigades achieved another major victory against the Houthis, seizing three districts in the southern governorate of Shabwa and advancing deeper into neighbouring Marib. Their offensive came to a halt after the Houthis launched an attack on Abu Dhabi on January 17, 2022.

Al-Muharrami had no known military background before the war, which began with the Houthis’ capture of Sanaa in September 2014, and the group has largely stayed out of infighting between anti-Houthi forces.

He joined Yemen’s eight-member PLC in April 2022, around the time his forces adopted the name Southern Giants Brigades, signalling their growing southern political identity. The formation later joined the STC, further strengthening the brigades’ ties with the southern separatist movement.

When STC forces collapsed following the Yemeni government offensive in January, al-Muharrami flew to Riyadh and voiced support for the Saudi-led initiative to unify southern forces.

The Giants Brigades’ involvement in the war against the Houthis is now seen as a test of its political allegiance, with some observers arguing that it remains fundamentally a separatist force.

Some believe that the Giants Brigades’ previous advances against the Houthis into Hodeidah suggest that the group does not necessarily have a separatist agenda.

They have also pointed to the group’s spearheading of the latest military offensive against the Houthis beyond southern Yemen, where many former STC units have remained confined, as another sign of its stronger commitment to national unity.

Fathi bin Lazraq, editor of the Aden Al-Ghad newspaper and an outspoken critic of southern separatists, believes that the Giants Brigades would be willing to fight the Houthis anywhere in Yemen.

“These forces are part of the contingent that has been fighting the Houthis since 2015, having been formed in Yemen following the collapse of the Yemeni army,” he told Al Jazeera. “They engage the Houthis from military, political, civil and religious standpoints.”

Bin Lazraq described the Giants Brigades as a powerful fighting force and pointed to their previous operations in northern areas, including Hodeidah and Marib. He also believes that the word “Southern” in their name did not necessarily mean they supported secession or would refuse to fight beyond the borders of the formerly independent South Yemen state.

But unlike Homeland Shield Forces, which were established by PLC head al-Alimi in January 2023 and placed under his direct command, making their allegiance to the internationally recognised government clear, the Giants Brigades operate in a more grey area.

“They do not fight as ‘Southern forces’ per se, but rather as part of the legitimate government forces backed by the [Saudi-led] coalition,” bin Lazraq said. “While they operate under the banner of southern forces, they do not claim to be separatist, or anything of the sort, given that they have fought in Hodeidah and Marib.”

The Giants Brigades, and even more hardline separatist STC-affiliated forces, had come to recognise the dangers posed by the Houthis and the need to ally with government forces to fight the group.

“Everyone believes that the Houthis pose a threat: if we do not go to them, they will come to us. The Giants Brigades and other forces are all united in a single battle to confront the Houthis,” he said.

But accusations that the Giants Brigades have southern separatist aspirations are also not unwarranted. The group’s current offensive is focused on areas within the borders of the former South Yemen entity, including the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

Some of their fighters taking part in the offensive around Bab al-Mandeb have raised the former South Yemen flag, and embedded journalists have also shared footage showing soldiers expressing southern separatist sentiments.

STC President Aidarous al-Zubaidi, who has not appeared publicly since the defeat of his forces in January, weighed into the debate by offering condolences for fighters killed in the offensive, describing them as martyrs, and criticising what he says is others taking credit for victories by southern forces.

“The South will not allow the victories of its armed forces to be stolen under slogans that do not reflect its reality,” al-Zubaidi said on X.

Anwar al-Tamimi, a spokesperson for the STC, told Al Jazeera that the participation of southern forces in the campaign was focused on capturing and securing the Bab al-Mandeb and surrounding areas, which separatists consider part of the state they seek to restore.

“The participation of southern forces is aimed at protecting and securing the south’s borders, a principle deeply rooted in southern military doctrine and central to the southern cause. Bab al-Mandeb falls within the territory of the former People’s Democratic Republic of Yemen,” he said.

Al-Tamimi did not rule out the possibility of southern forces advancing deeper into northern Yemen to secure their gains and borders, following similar military operations in the north.

The Giants Brigades remained loyal to the southern independence movement despite their participation in the wider anti-Houthi offensive.

“The Giants Brigades are southern brigades driven by a southern combat ethos, alongside elements of Salafist ideas,” al-Tamimi told Al Jazeera.

“This serves to reinforce the southern national project rather than bypass it. The Giants Brigades are a southern force; they carry the flag and banner of the south, and there is no issue with that. They are part of the southern armed forces – and a very active part at that.”

articles.title: ‘Energy ceasefire’: What’s behind Trump’s love-hate ties to Russian oil?
articles.summary: Trump’s energy truce sparks criticism over aiding Russia’s war finances amid diesel shortages and rising consumer costs.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has announced an immediate “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, days after easing sanctions on Russian fuel to tackle soaring domestic and global fuel prices.

The energy truce, announced on Sunday, marks another shift in Washington’s approach to Russian energy, as the Iran-US war and recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities disrupted global oil supplies and pushed up fuel prices. Trump has even asked Ukraine not to attack Russian oil facilities, as Moscow remains a major exporter of diesel.

The spike in diesel prices in recent weeks has particularly put pressure on Trump’s Republican Party ahead of November’s midterm elections. Surveys show Americans hold the Trump administration responsible for the soaring fuel prices amid the unpopular US war on Iran.

“Attacks on refineries and energy facilities have taken capacity out of an already stretched global fuel market, pushing up costs for transport, agriculture and businesses, with the pain ultimately passed on to consumers,” Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, told Al Jazeera, referring to the mutual attacks on energy sites by Ukraine and Russia.

“A genuine ceasefire could help protect supplies and ease some of that pressure, particularly as winter approaches.”

However, she warned it was too early to call it a “diplomatic breakthrough”, citing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s statement that the energy truce came as a surprise to him.

Trump’s decisions have drawn criticism from US politicians and European allies, who warn that allowing Russian fuel back into global markets could provide Moscow with new revenue to finance its war in Ukraine. In March, the Trump administration gave a sanctions waiver to Russian seaborne oil.

So, why has Trump repeatedly changed his position on Russian energy, and what is behind his latest decisions?

What is the ‘energy ceasefire’ Trump announced?

On Sunday, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to immediately stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure.

“Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social, without providing further details.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was not aware of the energy truce, saying the deal was “news to me” but welcomed the announcement nonetheless.

However, he said Russian drones continued targeting Ukrainian energy facilities, including a power plant in Kharkiv, after Trump’s statement.

“We are waiting for the details of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, ⁠⁠⁠⁠and we are waiting ⁠⁠⁠⁠to see one specific step the Americans are ready to take,” Zelenskyy said on Monday during a video address to a security conference in Warsaw.

“This ⁠⁠⁠⁠energy ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step towards ending ‌‌‌‌the war if the Americans truly step in now and make ‌‌‌‌sure ‌‌‌‌Russians respect it.”

Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian oil refineries, arguing that energy revenues help fund Moscow’s war . Russia, meanwhile, has attacked Ukraine’s electricity and heating infrastructure throughout the four-year conflict.

Academic Alexey Muriaev has urged caution over Trump’s announcement, questioning whether an agreement has actually been reached, and if so, what it entails.

“Is it about suspending attacks on oil refineries? And if that’s the case, then the situation would be inadequate, because Ukraine’s oil refineries have already been taken out by Russia’s strikes beforehand,” Muraviev, senior research fellow in Defence and Strategic Studies at Edith Cowan University, told Al Jazeera.

“So, in this sense, it would mean effectively Ukraine suspending unilateral action against Russia’s oil refinery facilities.”

Muriaev also linked the announcement to Trump’s diesel agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, suggesting it may be a signal to Zelenskyy.

“Attacking Russian oil refinery capability would probably be interpreted by Washington as an attack on US economic interests,” he said, referring to the agreement on diesel exports through April 2027.

The ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have continued to keep global oil markets under pressure.

On Monday, Brent crude, the international benchmark, fell to about $103.04 a barrel following Trump’s ceasefire announcement and Russian diesel deal, while US West Texas Intermediate crude traded at about $90.96.

However, prices remain elevated because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28, and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies flow.

Recent attacks on Saudi oil installations and airports by Yemen’s Houthis and the fighting around the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait have put further pressure on oil prices.

Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have compounded diesel shortages, affecting a fuel essential for the agriculture and trucking industries.

The crisis prompted the Group of Seven nations last week to agree to release 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel reserves. The G7 decision came after pressure from Trump.

How has the Trump administration zig-zagged between punishing and embracing Russian energy?

Washington’s approach to Russian energy has shifted repeatedly since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Under President Joe Biden, the US banned Russian oil and energy imports in March 2022, seeking to cut off revenue used to finance Moscow’s war.

But Washington simultaneously supported a G7 price cap on Russian oil, designed to restrict Moscow’s earnings without removing too much supply from global markets.

Moreover, the Biden administration also accepted India’s continued purchases of Russian crude to prevent global prices from rising.

After returning to power last year, Trump initially intensified pressure on Moscow. In August 2025, his administration imposed additional tariffs on Indian goods over New Delhi’s purchases of Russian oil.

Two months later, Washington sanctioned Russian energy giants Rosneft and Lukoil, accusing Moscow of failing to seriously pursue peace negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.

However, Washington’s approach took a dramatic turn this year. On March 5, Washington issued a 30-day waiver allowing India to buy Russian oil stranded at sea, as disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz amid US attacks on Iran threatened global supplies.

A week later, the Trump administration expanded the exemption, allowing countries worldwide to buy sanctioned Russian oil and petroleum products already loaded onto tankers, with the waiver lasting until April 11.

In September, Trump urged Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries, blaming the strikes for global diesel shortages.

On October 9, he announced an agreement with Russian President Putin for Moscow to release more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, with another 1.5 million tonnes to follow.

Why has Trump changed his position on Russian oil frequently?

Trump’s shifting public position on Russian energy reflects ongoing, and often competing, political and economic pressures.

“Trump is caught between his geopolitical ambitions and the domestic political consequences of expensive energy,” Susannah Streeter of Wealth Club, told Al Jazeera.

She said Washington was trying to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine while simultaneously allowing Russian fuel sales that could generate additional revenue for the Kremlin.

“The shift may deliver a short-term political gain if supplies increase and prices ease, but it could come at a longer-term diplomatic cost,” she said, adding that the benefits appeared limited while the Middle East war continued.

US diesel prices reached a record $6.52 per gallon in September, placing Trump under pressure ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

However, according to academic Muriev, the US president’s public rhetoric should be distinguished from his administration’s actions.

“I don’t really see inconsistency in Trump’s approach because, apart from his public rhetoric, apart from his frequent media posting, there’s been a more steady approach on behalf of his administration,” he told Al Jazeera.

He pointed to discussions between Russian and American officials in August and September, suggesting that negotiations over the latest diesel agreement may have begun well before Trump’s announcement last Friday.

Muriev suggested the timing of the announcement could be politically motivated, allowing Trump to claim a victory on energy prices before the midterms.

Moreover, Moscow also has an interest in helping Trump retain political influence because his administration appears more willing to negotiate with Russia than former President Biden was. Trump has been relatively more accepting of the Russian position on the Ukraine war and has even blamed Zelenskyy for failing to end the war.

“For Putin, it’s not just about scoring immediate economic benefit, but also achieving longer-term political and strategic goals,” Muriev said, referring to other issues such as Iran, cybersecurity, space cooperation and nuclear arms control.

The energy crisis has also created contrasting consequences for American businesses.

While higher oil prices can boost revenues for US energy producers, they increase operating costs for businesses dependent on fuel.

Susannah Streeter said cheaper diesel could provide relief to trucking companies, farmers and manufacturers, although the additional Russian supplies were unlikely to make a significant difference while disruptions in the Middle East continued.

She also warned that frequent changes to sanctions could create uncertainty for companies making long-term investment and supply-chain decisions.

“If sanctions are relaxed, reimposed or changed at short notice, companies face greater uncertainty over sourcing, compliance and the risk of being caught on the wrong side of a policy reversal,” she said.

articles.title: Azerbaijan’s school hijab ban: What’s behind it, and what’s next?
articles.summary: Protests have broken out as some schools begin preventing students and teachers from attending classes.
articles.body:
An Azerbaijan government decision to indirectly prohibit students and staff from wearing the hijab in schools has sparked protests.

The amendment approved last month stopped short of explicitly banning the Muslim headscarf but barred clothing in schools that the government said violates the “principle of secularism”.

The decision has sparked protests as some schools began preventing students and teachers from attending classes.

Teacher Zahra Hasanova told Al Jazeera that she was informed she could no longer wear the hijab at school. “To be honest, I am a little emotional. I am hurt,” she said. “[The hijab] is a personal choice, and if one day I want to take it off, that should be my choice too.”

The state-run Azerbaijani Press Agency (APA) said the amendment to the Descriptions of Uniforms for Students of State General Education Institutions aimed to ensure a unified dress code that reflects the country’s “secular principle”.

About 96 percent of Azerbaijan’s population identifies as Muslim. Its constitution defines the country as secular while also guaranteeing religious freedom.

The APA added that clothes that reflect the “history, culture, and national and moral values of the Azerbaijani people” may be worn for celebrations pending approval by the Pedagogical Council, which operates under the Ministry of Science and Education.

Such clothing ensures that teachers reflect “professional standards” and will have positive effects on the “school’s public reputation”, it said.

The measure has sparked protests and a social media campaign in Azerbaijan. Videos circulated showing students hugging their teachers and crying as they were turned away from schools.

Local media outlets reported that students in at least two schools in Azerbaijan boycotted classes in protest against the restrictions.

Imprisoned journalist Polad Aslanov, who is serving a 113-year prison sentence after being convicted of high treason in 2020, launched a hunger strike over the new requirements.

“Despite being in prison, I am raising my voice against the trampling of our constitutional rights by employing the only means of struggle available to me – a hunger strike!” Aslanov wrote in a message posted on Facebook by his wife, Gulmira Aslanova.

Reports of internet blackouts have not been confirmed by data from watchdogs, including Open Observatory of Network Interference and NetBlocks.

A social media campaign followed by protests also spread to Turkiye. Some have drawn parallels between the developments in Azerbaijan and Turkiye’s “post-modern coup” in 1997 when women wearing headscarves were banned from attending university classes and dismissed from their civil service jobs or were forced to resign.

Demonstrators last week gathered outside Azerbaijan’s consulate in Istanbul to protest the restrictions affecting Muslim women, calling on authorities in Baku to reconsider the decision.

Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev issued a veiled criticism of Turkiye, a strong ally of Azerbaijan, for the protests. In a speech at his New Azerbaijan Party congress, Aliyev warned not to “interfere with our lifestyle” without directly mentioning Turkiye.

Authorities in Ankara did not officially respond to Aliyev’s comment. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, however, mentioned in his September 23 address at the United Nations General Assembly that Muslim women were facing increasing discrimination.

articles.title: Vox rises as Sanchez battles political turmoil: Could Spain swing right?
articles.summary: Snap vote could bring PP, Vox to power as polls show falling support for Sanchez, one of Europe’s last leftist leaders.
articles.body:
Madrid, Spain – “What I really hate about [Prime Minister Pedro] Sanchez is how keen he is to allow more migrants into our country,” said Alberto Munoz, who wears the red and gold wristband of Vox party supporters.

The 24-year-old computer programmer from Barcelona is among a growing group of young Spanish people who are attracted to the far-right, anti-immigration party.

Eight years ago, Vox was a tiny party on the fringes of Spanish politics. But polls suggested it is getting closer to power as Spain heads to snap elections on November 29.

To reach a parliamentary majority, 176 seats are needed. According to a recent survey by the leading centre-left newspaper El Pais, the conservative People’s Party (PP) and Vox – whose support is predicted to double from the last elections in 2023 – would secure 198 seats. If the PP forms a coalition with Vox, it would be the first time the hard right would return to power in Spain since the death of Francisco Franco in 1975.

In the most recent elections in 2023, the PP won the most votes but not enough to lead on its own, and it did not enter a coalition with Vox. Sanchez of the Socialist Workers’ Party instead formed a government with the help of the Catalan nationalist party, Together for Catalonia.

Since then, the PP has formed four regional governments with Vox, and the parties share power in about 100 councils. A coalition between them now would likely see Sanchez defeated.

“There is hope for Spain with these elections. We will fight for victory and to convince Spaniards we are worth voting for,” Jose Antonio Fuster, national spokesman for Vox, told Al Jazeera. “But the PP cannot make the same mistakes as 2023 and must not start dividing up ministries until we have won.”

Sanchez’s party is predicted to win 112 seats in November, down from 121 three years ago.

If the Socialists lose, it would spell the end of one of the last left-wing governments left in Europe after advances for the far right in France, Germany, Italy, Austria and Finland as populism sweeps Europe.

Steven Forti, an expert in the far right who lectures in contemporary history at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, said, like other far-right parties in Europe and Latin America, Vox distances itself from the Franco dictatorship.

Santiago Abascal, the Vox leader, once told the Spanish parliament that Sanchez’s government was the “worst for the past 80 years” – implying the Franco dictatorship was better.

“It is dog whistle politics – you do not make an explicit reference to the dictatorship. Vox is like other far-right parties in that respect,” Forti told Al Jazeera.

“Young people are attracted to Vox by a feeling of rebellion against the established parties, nationhood and antimigrant feeling. If the polls are right, they will be in power with the PP, but what matters is what ministries they control.”

Vox is the only party that has substantially increased its support. A survey for RTVE, the state broadcaster, projected that the far-right party would increase its seats in parliament from 33 to 65 while it indicated the PP’s support had not risen and all left-wing parties had lost support.

Antonio Alonso, a lecturer in international relations at the University CEU San Pablo in Madrid, said right-wing parties were more stable than their badly divided opponents.

“What is key is that the far left is split into so many different groups and it will be hard to mobilise them as one front together. Meanwhile, the right with the PP and Vox is more unified,” he told Al Jazeera.

Alberto Nunez Feijoo, the PP leader, plans to play on voters’ anger over corruption scandals that have hit Sanchez.

“This is an election between corruption and decency, between decline and prosperity, between a government that aspires only to survive and a country that is thinking about its future,” he told reporters after Sanchez announced the snap elections.

He also pledged to build 200,000 homes each year and cut taxes.

Fired up by a housing crisis that has seen tens of thousands of people protest across Spain, Sanchez called the vote in an audacious gamble to rally support and confound the polls.

It was the eviction of 87-year-old Maria del Carmen Abascal from her Madrid home, a flat she had lived in for seven decades, which inflamed public opinion and prompted activists to camp out in central Madrid and other cities. Known across Spain as Maricarmen, she died this month after the protests.

When two government bills designed to protect people like Abascal were defeated in parliament, it prompted huge demonstrations, and Sanchez decided to capitalise on this tide of anger and call the elections.

Observers said Sanchez hopes the strength of feeling over the housing crisis might eclipse anger over corruption scandals involving members of his family, the perceived mishandling of the Ceuta migration crisis and an amnesty for Catalan separatists who led a failed independence bid in 2017.

The two defeated housing measures to protect tenants from eviction were later passed by the acting government.

“They protect the most vulnerable and, in some way, begin to bring order to what is currently a deeply dysfunctional market that does not operate according to the logic of supply and demand because of rampant speculation,” Sanchez told reporters.

However, even though Sanchez is renowned as a clever political operator, this gamble may not be enough. Even before Sanchez’s announcement of the elections, the Socialists had trailed in almost every opinion poll for months with most voters saying they would back the PP and Vox.

articles.title: Elton John’s foundation reached 523,000 people with HIV services in 68 countries as global funding cuts threatened clinics
articles.summary: The Elton John AIDS Foundation reached 523,000 people with HIV services across 68 countries in 2025. Progress Needs Protecting.
articles.body: The Elton John AIDS Foundation reached 523,000 people with HIV services across 68 countries in 2025. Progress Needs Protecting. Global funding cuts disrupted healthcare services, with clinics closing, prevention programmes stopping and communities facing barriers to essential care. During the year, it tested 230,692 people for HIV, distributed 57,688 self-test kits and initiated 26,857 people on pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). It also awarded 44 grants totalling $18,768,059 and expanded the Rocket Fund to $200 million in September 2025 to address growing needs.How global funding cuts threatened HIV treatment programmesAccording to the Elton John AIDS Foundation’s report, the global HIV response entered one of its most challenging periods in early 2025 after international funding was withdrawn. According to the welcome letter from Elton John, David Furnish and Anne Aslett, “Clinics closed their doors. Health workers were sent home. Prevention programs stopped overnight.” The report also states that millions of people living with or at risk of HIV were left without the treatment and care needed to sustain their health. These disruptions affected services at a time when communities were already facing stigma, criminalisation and poverty.In March 2025, the foundation launched the Rocket Response Fund to prevent interruptions to HIV services following cuts to United States foreign aid. The annual report states that “Around two-thirds of partners in Africa and Asia reported immediate disruptions”, including clinic closures, suspended laboratory services, medication shortages and halted prevention programmes. The fund supported interventions intended to maintain access to essential healthcare. The report documents support for LGBTQ+-friendly health centres in Uganda, staffing and laboratory testing in Vietnam, HIV testing kits and condoms in Cameroon, and hotline counselling for LGBTQ+ communities in the Philippines.How the foundation supported HIV testing and treatment in 2025The foundation reported awarding 44 grants totalling $18,768,059 in 2025 to support community-led initiatives. Its annual impact figures recorded 230,692 people tested for HIV, alongside the distribution of 57,688 self-test kits. The foundation also reported initiating 20,984 people on antiretroviral therapy (ART), which is used to treat HIV. These figures formed part of its reported efforts to expand access to diagnosis, treatment and prevention services across the countries where its partners operated.Prevention was another component of the foundation’s work. During 2025, it initiated 26,857 people on pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), a medication used to prevent HIV infection, and funded PrEP programmes across 26 countries. The report also recorded 52,199 people connected with mental health services and 9,686 healthcare providers, advocates and changemakers trained. According to the report, these activities were intended to strengthen frontline services and improve the quality of care for communities most affected by HIV.How Elton John’s foundation expanded the Rocket Fund to $200 millionThe foundation also reported expanding the Rocket Fund to $200 million in September 2025 in response to escalating global needs. The annual report describes the fund as a long-term approach focused on innovative, community-led programmes for people most at risk of HIV. Its five strategic priorities include advancing rights and inclusion, strengthening community movements, innovating for equitable healthcare access, reaching underserved communities and mobilising additional funding. The report states that, since 2020, the Rocket Fund and its partners had reached more than 2.49 million people, including 696,000 young people, across 76 countries through more than 285 grants.Scientific developments also featured prominently in the foundation’s account of the year. In their welcome letter, the foundation’s leaders highlighted twice-yearly injections that prevent HIV, describing them as a significant development in prevention. The report cautions that scientific progress must be accompanied by access to ensure that new interventions reach the people who need them. It also describes the foundation’s work with partners across sub-Saharan Africa to improve access to long-acting injectable PrEP for young women and LGBTQ+ communities.How Elton John’s foundation supported HIV programmes in 55 countriesThe 2025 annual report presents the foundation’s work as a combination of emergency support, prevention, treatment, mental health services and longer-term investment in community organisations. It records 133 funded programmes with grants spanning 68 countries during the year. The foundation also reported supporting community-led movements, networks and coalitions in 55 countries, alongside programmes advancing legal protections and the rights of people living with or affected by HIV in 21 countries.The foundation emphasised the importance of maintaining support for HIV services and ensuring that advances in prevention reach affected communities. Elton John, the foundation’s founder, said in the annual report: “The world can end AIDS. What is missing is courage. The courage not to look away.” The report presents the foundation’s 2025 results against a backdrop of international funding disruption, highlighting its recorded reach of 523,000 people with HIV services across 68 countries and its continued investment in programmes addressing prevention, treatment and barriers to care.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2019, Emma Watson helped launch a free workplace harassment advice line; seven years later, women in England and Wales can still use the service for specialist help with their legal rights
articles.summary: British actor and activist Emma Watson has helped support the launch of a free legal advice service for women facing sexual harassment at work in England
articles.body: British actor and activist Emma Watson has helped support the launch of a free legal advice service for women facing sexual harassment at work in England and Wales. The service, introduced by the charity Rights of Women, was designed to help women understand their legal rights and the steps they could take against workplace harassment. Seven years later, the advice line continues to operate, offering specialist legal guidance to women dealing with such situations.The service was launched in 2019, with funding from the TIME’S UP UK Justice and Equality Fund. Watson was among those whose donations helped establish the fund, which was managed by Rosa, the UK Fund for Women and Girls. The initiative followed the global 'MeToo' movement, during which millions of women shared their experiences of sexual harassment and abuse.According to Rights of Women, the helpline is the only free specialist legal advice line of its kind for women experiencing sexual harassment at work in England and Wales. The charity also cited research by the Trades Union Congress (TUC), which found that as many as one in two women had experienced sexual harassment in the workplace.The aim was to make legal advice more accessible to women who might otherwise struggle to understand their options or take action against harassment.How Emma Watson became involved Watson supported the initiative through the TIME’S UP UK Justice and Equality Fund, which was established with donations from the public and supporters, including the actor.The money helped Rights of Women establish a dedicated telephone service staffed by its legal team and volunteer women employment lawyers. The advisers were tasked with explaining workplace harassment laws and helping callers understand the legal action available to them.Speaking at the launch in 2019, Watson welcomed the initiative but expressed concern that such a service had not been available earlier.“It’s completely staggering to think that this is the only service of its type given that research has found that as many as one in two women experience sexual harassment in the workplace,” she said.Watson also stressed that understanding legal rights was an important part of addressing workplace harassment. “Understanding what your rights are, how you can assert them, and the choices you have if you’ve experienced harassment, is such a vital part of creating safe workplaces for everyone,” she said.Need for legal adviceWhen the service was introduced, Rights of Women said many women experiencing workplace harassment were reluctant to complain because they feared the consequences for their careers.Deeba Syed, then Senior Legal Officer at Rights of Women, said harassment had often been treated as something women were expected to tolerate at work. She also pointed to the shortage of specialist legal support for those who wanted to challenge such behaviour.According to the charity, women reporting harassment could face negative responses, have their complaints undermined or experience victimisation. The advice line was intended to help them understand the law before deciding what action to take.It also formed part of the organisation's wider efforts to address the barriers that made it difficult for women to report harassment and hold employers accountable.Workplace harassment law changed in 2024Since the advice line was launched, workplace harassment protections in the UK have also changed. Rights of Women says it successfully campaigned for changes introduced through the Worker Protection Act 2024. From October 26, 2024, employers became legally required to take reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment of their employees.According to the charity, failure to meet this duty may result in an additional compensation award of up to 25% for employees who have experienced sexual harassment, where the relevant legal conditions are met.Rights of Women also encourages women to report workplace sexual harassment to the EHRC, which has regulatory powers to act against employers and may support litigation.Women in England and Wales can contact the Sexual Harassment at Work Advice Line on 020 7490 0152. According to the charity's website, the service operates on Mondays, Tuesdays and Wednesdays from 6pm to 8pm, and on Thursdays and Fridays from 10am to 12pm, UK time.You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump thinks Ukraine needs a new president. Who could replace Zelenskyy?
articles.summary: Popular former general Zaluzhnyi leads potential challengers, alongside intelligence chief Budanov and reformer Fedorov.
articles.body:
Kyiv, Ukraine – The White House wants Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy gone.

“I think it’s ⁠⁠time for Ukraine to get a new president,” United States President Donald Trump told reporters on Saturday, claiming that Zelenskyy’s months-long strikes on Russian refineries had hurt global diesel supplies.

But Trump’s wish is not Ukraine’s command.

Even though Zelenskyy’s five-year presidential term expired in 2024, Ukraine’s constitution and martial law grant him a wartime extension. Many Ukrainians want their political establishment to be renewed, but are reluctant to see a presidential vote before the four-and-a-half year war is over.

In response to Trump’s remarks, Zelenskyy proposed holding a vote if Russian President Vladimir Putin guaranteed a 60-day ceasefire.

However, if the elections are held in the near future, who could compete with Zelenskyy?

“If the elections are held fast, one of the former military [commanders] is Zelenskyy’s most probable rival,” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevych told Al Jazeera.

Meanwhile, old political heavyweights such as former President Viktor Poroshenko, who lost the 2019 presidential vote to Zelenskyy, and former Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko, who is being investigated for corruption, do not stand a chance, he said.

Valerii Zaluzhnyi: ‘Most probable alternative’

Ukraine’s former top general and current ambassador to the United Kingdom tops the lists of Zelenskyy’s rivals.

“At least since 2023, and especially since 2024, after his resignation, the most probable alternative to Zelenskyy, his most dangerous competitor who can defeat him in the election is Valerii Zaluzhnyi,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera.

Almost two-thirds of Ukrainians – 64 percent – trust him, according to an October 8 poll by the Rating Group, a Kyiv-based pollster, and only 25 percent “distrust” him.

This trust is rooted in his 2022 military triumphs.

After defending Kyiv in the early weeks of Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, Zaluzhnyi led counteroffensives that returned 40 percent of Russian-controlled territory to Ukraine.

He was fired in 2023 after a long-anticipated summer counteroffensive yielded no results.

Zaluzhnyi remains a man of mystery when it comes to the most pressing postwar matters.

Burly and imposing, the 53-year-old is deliberately taciturn, leaving the public guessing about his views on Ukraine’s economic restoration, crippling demographic crisis or push to join the European Union.

He does not take part in talk shows, barely talks to journalists and occasionally publishes opinion pieces with detailed analyses of war-related problems and general statements about securing lasting peace and security guarantees from Ukraine’s Western partners.

The former comedian was elected in 2019 with 73 percent of the vote, the highest result in Ukraine’s post-Soviet history.

Despite a string of corruption scandals in his inner circle, the 48-year-old is popular enough to take another swing at a presidency.

More than half of Ukrainians – 53 percent – trust him, although 40 percent do not, according to the Rating Group’s poll.

However, Trump’s renewed animosity may benefit Zelenskyy again.

After his February 2025 row with Trump in the Oval Office, Zelenskyy’s approval ratings hit a wartime high of 67 percent.

However, Zelenskyy may have ruined his own chances with his appointment policies.

“He came to power under the slogans of resetting the power, of picking the most competent, not the most trusted” ministers or advisers, analyst Tyshkevych said.

Kyrylo Budanov: Trusted by more than half of Ukrainians

Lt. Gen. Kyrylo Budanov is the second most popular and charismatic military leader who has a shot at becoming Ukraine’s president.

The 40-year-old former top military intelligence officer was appointed head of Zelenskyy’s administration in January.

Budanov led daring operations against Russia, including a raid on Russian-annexed Crimea in 2016 to plant explosives at a military airfield.

In 2020, Zelenskyy appointed him head of the defence ministry’s intelligence directorate (GUR), which became an aggressive, tech-driven special forces service.

The GUR’s sea drone attacks damaged Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, forcing it to retreat from annexed Crimea to the Russian port of Novorossiysk.

Budanov is trusted by 53 percent of Ukrainians and mistrusted by 31 percent, according to the Rating Group’s poll.

Mykhailo Fedorov: Young, popular, daring

At 35, Fedorov is the youngest person on the list of potential presidents. He rose to fame after Zelenskyy appointed him minister of digital transformation in 2019, and managed to radically simplify bureaucratic procedures in the corruption-plagued nation. His ministry launched Diia, a smartphone app that lets users access more than 100 government services online.

In January, Zelenskyy appointed Fedorov, who had zero military background, as defence minister in charge of logistics, budgets, reforms, anticorruption measures and deals to secure multibillion-dollar Western aid or loans.

Fedorov cracked down on corruption schemes by making procurement of new weaponry, food and medical supplies more transparent.

He radically boosted the number of drones that paralysed Russia’s supply routes, destroyed arms and fuel depots, oil refineries and air defence systems.

He also increased the number of ground robots to supply food and ammunition and rescue wounded soldiers.

But the reforms angered Oleksandr Syrsky, the actual commander-in-chief, who reportedly pushed for Fedorov’s dismissal in July.

Fedorov’s supporters rallied throughout Ukraine for weeks, while his approval ratings soared from 35 percent in June to 65 percent in July, according to the Rating Group’s polls.

However, in August he made an unpopular move saying Ukraine should hold a presidential vote, and his current approval stands at 38 percent.

Yevhenii Khmara: Ukraine’s unknown defence minister

The top five list ends with Yevhenii Khmara, a general who replaced Fedorov as defence minister.

A relative unknown until his appointment in July, he is trusted by 29 percent of Ukrainians and distrusted by 16 percent.

He was a career intelligence official with a low public profile, but another 43 percent of those polled did not know who he was, according to the survey.

Low hopes for a foreign minister and an ex-president

Numbers six and seven on the list are Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, a career diplomat who secured crucial support from Turkiye and Poland, and ex-president Poroshenko.

Both are trusted by 24 percent of Ukrainians.

But Poroshenko, who came to power in 2014 on an anti-corruption ticket but got involved in a graft scandal with overpriced spare parts for military equipment, holds a low popularity rating – 70 percent of those polled distrust him.

articles.title: American entrepreneur Jason Lee Beckwith buys abandoned Spanish village Salto de Castro for €310,000 and plans to revive its 44 homes, church, school and bar
articles.summary: Picture an entire village standing silent above a river, its houses empty, its school without pupils and its bar without customers.
articles.body: Picture an entire village standing silent above a river, its houses empty, its school without pupils and its bar without customers. Now picture an American couple walking through it and deciding to bring it back to life. That is the story of Salto de Castro, a settlement in western Spain that stood abandoned for more than three decades before a Californian entrepreneur bought it. Here’s how the purchase happened, what the village contains, how much money is involved, how residents might fit into the plan, and what the proposed project could mean for the future of rural Spain.How Jason Beckwith went from running guesthouses in California to buying an abandoned Spanish villageBeckwith told El País that he opened a guesthouse, sold it five years later, took a sabbatical year and then decided with his wife to open another, which is when he found Zamora. Medium, in an interview with him, reports that in spring 2024 he and his wife, Ana Cristina Machado, were looking for a new hospitality project when he read that Salto de Castro was for sale. Despite speaking no Spanish and knowing no one locally, he flew to Madrid that summer, took a fast train to Zamora and drove to the village. Beckwith told Knauss, "Something in me has been chasing something like this all my life." He also told El País that he bought an apartment in Zamora and hopes to live full-time beside the Douro.What Salto de Castro contains, from 44 homes, a church and a school to a bar, former barracks and a swimming poolAccording to the Idealista real estate listing, as described by El País, the village includes homes, five of them stand-alone, plus a bar, a church, a school with several classrooms, a laundry room, a former Civil Guard barracks, a swimming pool and sports facilities. The listing also notes a guesthouse with up to fourteen rooms approved for building. Polsat News, citing the Spanish newspaper El Cronista, counts 44 homes in total. El País reports that the electricity company Iberduero, now Iberdrola, built the village in 1946, and that it was abandoned in 1989 after the last power station workers and Civil Guard officers were transferred out. Ángel Encinas, who spent his early years there, told El País that the school was his first and is very well built.How much the village cost and what a full restoration could totalMedium reports the price as 310,000 euros, which at recent exchange rates is roughly $363,000. He paid half up front, with the rest due when the sale is final. El País says earlier owners estimated restoration at two million dollars. In contrast, Beckwith told the newspaper it can cost as high as seven million euros, with a detailed budget due after the summer. As per Medium, investors are offered half a per cent of equity for every 50,000 euros and are promised thirty-five jobs. Beckwith also told El País that he is seeking investors worldwide and subsidies because he believes the Spanish government and the European Union want to repopulate deserted regions.What Beckwith plans to build, from a vacation complex and long-term rentals to weddings in the churchEl País reports that Beckwith envisions a large vacation complex, either a hotel or a hostel, together with long-term rentals for people who want to live in the village full-time. Inside the church, he intends to hold weddings and concerts as well as religious services. He hopes the first phase will open within two years, with a main building of accommodations, a multi-level restaurant, a space for vendors, a welcome centre, a pool and recreation area, and a barbecue and picnic area. Beckwith told El País that local families will be able to swim and picnic there, adding, "Everyone will be welcome in my village." He rejects the idea of a glass-and-steel luxury development and describes a gradual ten-year plan.Why Salto de Castro remains uninhabitable in 2026 as the mayor, a former resident and ecologists reactSergio López, mayor of Fonfría, told El País in May 2025 that no formal request had yet been filed, though he welcomed the plan with great excitement and open arms. Ángel Encinas told the newspaper he supported slow, sustainable tourism within the limits of the natural park, while Ecologists in Action Castilla y León told El País a tourist complex conflicts with conservation goals. A Men's Journal report, dated 29 August 2026, says Beckwith still has not moved into the village while restoration is being planned. He and his wife live in an apartment in Zamora, though they are officially registered as residents of Salto de Castro, the first in decades. Men's Journal adds that he intends to relocate there and that environmental groups are watching closely.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: WWE star Drew McIntyre stars in micro-drama series 'Agent of Shadows,' touts company's reach beyond wrestling
articles.summary: Drew McIntyre plays a dangerous secret agent in "Agent of Shadows" on ReelShort, joined by Chase Mattson and several other WWE superstars.
articles.body: WWE star Drew McIntyre has already proved just how menacing he can be in the ring. He’s a four-time world champion, two-time tag team champion and one-time intercontinental champion. He’s won the Royal Rumble and Money in the Bank one time each as well. With his hulking figure and silky smooth long hair, it almost seems like the Scotsman was made for the cameras. Over the last year, he’s begun to prove that notion. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE McIntyre has had a role in the 2024 film "The Killer’s Game" and is set to be a part of "The Last Druid" starring Russell Crowe and the "Highlander" reboot, which also stars Crowe and WWE Hall of Famer Dave Bautista. With his recent success, McIntyre has gotten a part in a micro-drama series with actor Chase Mattson and a few other WWE figures. McIntyre stars as a dangerous secret agent. He goes undercover to help protect a young girl from being targeted by a billionaire arms dealer. But what makes "Agent of Shadows" stand out from every other TV show in the same genre, is that it will premiere on ReelShort. ReelShort is a streaming service that produces short-form videos for the social media age. McIntyre told OutKick Dropkick he was aware of the platform because he would need to watch something on airplanes as he traveled around the world for wrestling and filming. "I had a look at it, it was a lot of fun, a lot of chance to show some range, and I went, heck yeah, I wanna be part of this thing," he recalled after getting asked whether he would want to perform in the series. "It has the action, the comedy and it has heart, too." Mattson told OutKick Dropkick he was drawn to the show because of his martial-arts background. "I just felt like Adam, the character, was a lot like myself and I loved how much I could resonate with it so fast. I love the amount of action, comedy and a little bit of romance that was spread throughout the script. I was like, I need to be a part of this. And it was a lot different from all of the other projects that I’ve done." Mattson said he didn’t really know much about McIntyre before working with him. He noticed how big the pro wrestler. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "I’m like, OK, I’m 6-3, 215, I’m a big guy, too," he recalled. "But he walked on set and I was like, ‘This dude’s a giant.’ I’m big, that’s a giant. But no, I didn’t know anything about him other than that – he was a big guy. And he came and I was like, ‘OK, he’s probably going to be really mean.’ But he’s the nicest guy I’ve ever met. "I felt really honored to be acting alongside Drew because he had just came off of these movies with these big, heavy hitters and I’m like, ‘Oh you’re with me. This is kinda cool.’" WWE will have a massive imprint on "Agent of Shadows." The trailer for the micro-drama dropped last week. WWE stars like Royce Keys, Joe Hendry, Jacob Fatu, Nikkita Lyons, Hank Walker and Tank Ledger make an appearance. Michael Hayes and Booker T also make a splash in the show. McIntyre agreed that it shows that WWE is not just one thing when it comes to sports entertainment. It very much is sports and entertainment across the board. "Not one thing is an understatement, or understatement of the year these days," he said. "I first came into the company in ’07 and I could not imagine it being any bigger and to watch the growth from then to now and seeing the company everywhere in 180 countries, 28 different languages, 800 million homes, billions with a ‘B’ social media followers, on ESPN, Netflix, billion-dollar deals cut by the billion-dollar man Nick Khan and now getting involved in the vertical-short world with ReelShort … this is not a new thing, this is a billion-dollar industry and it’s awesome. "WWE is getting involved, giving our superstars a chance to showcase a different side of their personality in a more acting range with the action with the comedy and hopefully highlight using our platform to highlight, using the platform, a lot of the actors like Chase because it is the future no matter how anyone looks at it." articles.title: Northern Israel explosion kills at least 1 person, injures 19
articles.summary: The blast occurred in northern Israel near the Lebanese border and is under investigation.
articles.body:
One person has been killed and 19 others were injured in an explosion in northern Israel near the Lebanese border, according to preliminary official tallies, in an incident that is under investigation.

“I share in the heavy grief of the family of the boy who was killed in the explosion during the trip near the northern border, and I wish a swift and full recovery to all the injured,” Israel’s Defence Minister Israel Katz posted on X, adding that authorities were looking into the cause of the blast.

Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the victim was a 15-year-old who had gone on an annual school trip.

Citing medical sources, the Israeli police earlier said that “the initial suspicion is that it was caused by an unexploded ordnance, as a result of which about 20 people were injured with varying degrees of severity.” The explosion occurred near the community of Neot Mordechai, between Kibbutz Manara and Kibbutz Yiftach.

The incident injured both students and staff from a religious high school as they were on an outing, the municipality of the northern city of Maalot-Tarshiha said.

There is a heavy military deployment in the north of the country and in parts of southern Lebanon as Israel continues attacks it says target the Iran-aligned Hezbollah group.

Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank said that some of the injured are described to be in critical condition.

“There is very little specific information as to what happened, what the source of that explosion was, but it’s certainly a reminder that Northern Israel, the upper Galilee and particularly the border with Lebanon remains an area where there is a military operation, with the Israeli military deployed and where thousands of munitions were used over the past 3 years”, Odeh said.

Odeh said the explosion had “mobilised” Israel’s political echelons, with the Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu heading to the area, and the Israeli minister of National Security National Ben Gvir canceling a political engagement that was on his agenda.

Tens of thousands of Israelis living in the country’s north were forced to leave the region after Lebanon’s Hezbollah group started firing rockets following Israel’s genocidal 2023 war in Gaza.

In March, Israeli forces started occupying southern Lebanon following a renewal of hostilities after the US – Israel war on Iran. The military said soldiers and helicopters had been dispatched to the scene in northern Israel, a region from which Israeli forces have been pounding Lebanon, whose Hezbollah militants have fired periodic rockets across the border.

Odeh says most residents have not returned because they “did not have the confidence” that the government will be able to protect them.

“They saw the extensive damage that rockets were exacting on their communities and many them, according reports, have not been encouraged to return because the situation remains volatile”, she said.
